item.title: AI and Communications of the ACM
item.dc:creator: James Larus
item.description: When you finish writing your Communications article, give it to AI and ask it to act as an experienced, demanding editor and suggest improvements.
item.content:encoded:
Like many people, I’ve struggled to find an appropriate role for AI in Communications. Many, if not most, of our authors use AI to prepare their articles. According to ACM policies,a authors may use AI to write their articles and need not declare its use (by contrast, AI use in research still needs to be described in the methodology section). Still, some articles provoke a vocal response, with critics accusing them of being “AI Slop”—a vague but heavily pejorative label claiming that a machine wrote an article, that it contains commonplace observations, and that it lacks human insight. In some cases, the evidence appears to be little more than grammatically correct, stylistically polished prose.

I should note that, unlike almost all of ACM’s other publications, Communications articles are heavily edited by a professional staff. We have done this since the beginning to ensure readability and to maintain a “house style” appropriate for a magazine. Despite what some believe, many academics do not write easily or well. They can write a stylized technical paper for their colleagues, but they struggle to explain their research to a general audience. Professional editing can produce the polished prose that readers sometimes mistake for AI involvement, yet Communications’ editing has never provoked such complaints.

So, what is going on, and what should Communications do about it? Reversing ACM policy is not an option and would be a bad idea. AI is extremely helpful for writing, both for people who write frequently and, even more so, for those learning to write or writing in a non-native language. (In the interest of full disclosure, I use it to edit and improve my prose, and now I could no more imagine writing without it than driving without online maps, finding information without a search engine, typing a paper on a typewriter, or mailing a physical letter.)

The first explanation, and the one that concerns me most, is that the critics were correct: The submitted articles were poor, and we accepted them because they read well. Communications is selective; we reject approximately 80% of submitted articles. The idea of reviewing, especially for an edited magazine, is that reviewers should look beyond an article’s surface presentation and evaluate the quality of its ideas. But reviewers are human, and well-written articles are easier to digest and comment on, so perhaps a poor but very well-written article will get an undeserved boost.

The second explanation may reflect broader concerns about AI—its training, economic consequences, environmental costs, or its effect on the relationship between authors and readers—rather than the quality of a particular article. None of the objections explicitly raised this issue. Still, a recent Communications article about the organization’s policy on the ACM Digital Library and training LLMsb drew hundreds of responses, many of which were extremely critical of AI, so some readers have strong negative feelings about the technology.

The third explanation is that AI entirely wrote these articles in response to a high-level prompt, such as “write a Communications article on the topic of gold-plated foobars.” In this case, the human delegates both thinking and writing to AI. The result may be a well-written presentation of a topic, but it is unlikely to say anything, since AI does not (yet) have ideas of its own and so follows the well-trodden path of the material it was trained on. A system responding to a high-level prompt can synthesize familiar arguments fluently, but it has no research results, professional experience, or distinctive judgment to convey. These articles lack a message for the reader.

The fourth, and least satisfactory, explanation is that people find it unsettling to read an article bearing a human’s name that was clearly written by a machine. A similar phenomenon, called the “uncanny valley,” has long been observed in the robotics community, which has noted that machines that come close to lifelike disturbed humans far more than equivalent mechanisms that looked like machines. Perhaps a similar uncanny valley exists for intellectual artifacts such as articles. A byline establishes a relationship between an author and a reader, and readers may feel deceived when prose presented as an individual’s expression is produced by a machine.

As Communications Editor-in-Chief, I offer a few promises and pieces of advice. Communications will continue to accept and publish articles written with AI. We will apply the same standards of originality, substance, accuracy, and relevance, regardless of how the prose was produced or how polished it is. We will also hold human authors fully responsible for every claim, citation, and conclusion. For Communications, the important distinction is not between articles written with and without AI. It is between using AI to express human thought and using AI to avoid human thought.

Authors can help us by using AI to communicate their ideas better, not to produce a “push-button” submission on a topic:

  • If you write with AI’s assistance, do not stop. AI is not necessary to write a great Communications article, but it is a great tool for improving your writing and an even better editor. When you finish your Communications article, give it to AI and ask it to act as an experienced, demanding editor and suggest improvements. After revising the article thoughtfully, perhaps several times, ask AI to act as an experienced, strict Communications reviewer and criticize your piece. Then fix it and send it to us.

  • Do not let AI do your thinking for you. If you ask AI to write an article on a topic, it will produce a well-crafted piece, but it is unlikely to say anything interesting. The next person to use the AI could produce a substantially similar, if not identical, article. If you plan to submit an article to Communications, you should have ideas and results you want to share. AI can help, but you need to tell it what to do.

  • Remember that your name is on the article; AI’s name isn’t (and can’t be). You are personally responsible for everything in the article. Read AI’s output carefully and thoughtfully to ensure it reflects your views and is accurate. A byline is not a record of who typed the words. It declares intellectual ownership and responsibility—and AI does not change that.

item.title: Peering Into the Privacy of Smart Glasses
item.dc:creator: Rina Diane Caballar
item.description: Researchers, providers, and consumers are keeping a close eye on the devices' surveillance features.
item.content:encoded:
Smart glasses are making a spectacle.

These AI-augmented devices can see, hear, and understand a wearer’s surroundings, answering questions, dictating directions, and translating conversations. For people who are blind or have low vision, smart glasses can prove transformative,a helping them navigate their surroundings and complete certain tasks on their own.

Yet the wearable tech also puts privacy risks in plain view. Reports have surfaced of people using camera-equipped eyewear to surreptitiously film those around them,b later posting the recorded footage on social media.c Some videos might even be fed to AI models for training and, in some cases, may be subject to human review.

“The amount of data that these smart glasses are collecting is a lot more than people probably realize,” said Milica Stilinovic, a postdoctoral research associate at the University of Sydney in Australia who focuses on technological harms and the governance of emerging technologies. She has raised concerns around how data from glasses is stored and used, and around questionable data retention practices.

Glimpses of Privacy

Some companies are attempting to solve these issues. HTC’s Vive Eagle glasses,d for instance, won’t record unless they’re physically worn, and includes a feature that lets a person nearby say “stop recording” to instantly end the footage. Others have removed cameras altogether, such as Mira’s AI glasses,e which only keep transcripts without recording or storing audio.

However, Stilinovic regards these as “stopgap measures aiming to address the market in a way that doesn’t essentially eradicate the problem.”

A more apt solution entails wearable tech creators integrating privacy from the start, according to Lorrie Cranor, director and Bosch Distinguished Professor of the CyLab Security and Privacy Institute at Carnegie Mellon University. “They should put privacy front and center in the design process,” said Cranor, who’s also an ACM Fellow and a member of the ACM CHI Academy.

Privacy by design acts as a guiding principle for Raven Resonance, the company said. The startup is crafting Raven Prism, which founder Thomas Suarez likens to “a full computer on your face” that a wearer can control using their eyes and voice. He envisions a spatial future where instead of displaying apps on a screen, they exist as 3D objects “that are ambient around you, and they’re just there when you need them and gone when you don’t.”

Raven Prism, which is set to launch this fall, incorporates privacy features that blend restriction with indication: a colored physical camera cover that must be manually swiveled up, a bright red ring around the camera, and “Beakon” lights (named after a bird’s beak, in keeping with the bird theme) around the frame’s bottom rims that fade in and out in certain colors depending on whether the camera or microphone is turned on. Wearers can run small AI models locally, Suarez said, and since processing happens on-device, data stays on-device too.

“Smart glasses have more sensors and radios that can peer into people’s private lives than any personal computing device in history,” Suarez wrotef in detailing the team’s design decisions. “This is a major responsibility for anyone building in the wearable computing space. Our team is strongly against having any part in the creation of a device that promotes surveillance.”

Safeguards in Sight

With smart glasses, there’s more to privacy than meets the eye. It needs to be weaved into what the wearables sense, compute, retain, and communicate to those around them, said Faraz Faruqi, a recent Ph.D. graduate at MIT’s Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory whose research focused on human-computer interaction, generative AI, and interactive systems.

“Designers can ask what information a feature actually needs,” Faruqi said. “Not every capability requires a high-resolution image; depth, infrared, lower-resolution imaging, or other sensing modalities may sometimes provide enough information while capturing less identity-rich data.”

Raw sensor data can be processed within a constrained environment on the device and can be ephemeral rather than automatically stored, Faruqi suggested. Citing navigation as an example, he noted that a device might say “there’s a step ahead” by inferring information from the captured street image or video instead of directly accessing the underlying camera feed and without retaining the image or video.

Stilinovic recommends additional protective methods, such as blurring the faces of bystanders, opt-out mechanisms for collecting data, and stronger oversight. “We need to have particular regulatory measures that address the contemporary realities of this tech,” she added, including updating understanding of privacy and consent in the era of AI glasses.

For Cranor, participatory designg of both wearers and nonwearers remains vital, plus considering helpful use cases and the least amount of information required to fulfill them. “We need to have a framework for what is acceptable, what is not acceptable, and how to minimize the unnecessary recording and action on data that’s beyond the use case.”

Faruqi expressed similar sentiments: “A better goal is to design glasses that collect only the sensory information they need, process more of it locally, retain less of it, and communicate clearly to both wearers and bystanders what they are doing. Privacy therefore also means making sensing and recording legible to bystanders and thinking about what meaningful agency they can have when they are being sensed by someone else’s device.”

A Blurry Outlook

Looking to the future, Stilinovic said she doubted smart glasses will become a fixture in everyday lives. “Currently, the harms are outweighing the benefits,” she observed.

A backlash seems to be growing, with consumer venues introducing policies to restrict the technology, countries weighing bans in government workplaces and public spaces, and courts and schools barring their use. Some retailers have even halted salesh of Meta’s Ray-Ban smart glasses.

“I know we’ve heard from tech companies that smart glasses will be the natural extension of the human experience,” Stilinovic said, “but unless those privacy issues are addressed, I don’t see them being of benefit in the future.”

Cranor, on the other hand, said “We don’t have to go to the extreme of just banning smart glasses. I don’t think it’s all or nothing; I think we need to figure out how we can have them without them being complete tools of surveillance.”

The potential ubiquity of smart glasses, Faraz said, will depend on “how we develop technical safeguards and social norms that make people around them comfortable with their presence.” With today’s smartphones, for instance, raising them to take a photo or video is a visible and recognizable signal. But for smart glasses, “many of those cues are different,” he said, “so new technical mechanisms and social norms will have to develop alongside the technology.”

b. https://www.theguardian.com/technology/ng-interactive/2026/aug/19/meta-glasses-privacy-surveillance

c. https://fortune.com/2026/07/28/ray-ban-meta-pervert-glasses-secret-videos-women/

d. https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2026-09-03/htc-brings-its-smart-glasses-to-u-s-as-privacy-backlash-grows

g. https://cacm.acm.org/opinion/everything-everywhere-all-pervasive-augmented-reality/

Rina Diane Caballar is a freelance tech and science writer based in New Zealand.

item.title: Tailoring Elective Courses to Enhance Women’s Participation in Computing
item.dc:creator: Naaz Sibia
item.description: Enrollment patterns in elective classes offer actionable insight into how curricula might be redesigned to broaden participation in computing education.
item.content:encoded:
The underrepresentation of women in computing is not just a numerical imbalance; it is a significant loss of potential innovation, creativity, and progress. Despite technology’s omnipresence and the explosive growth of the tech industry, women remain markedly underrepresented in many computing programs across the world. According to UNESCO, women constitute only 28% of engineering graduates and 40% of computer science and informatics graduates globally.29 In Europe, women earn approximately 20% of information and communication technology bachelor’s degrees,26 while in the U.S., they account for only 22% of computing bachelor’s degrees.25 More recent national data show this gap has not significantly improved: in 2023, just 23% of U.S. computing degrees at the bachelor’s level were awarded to women.1 These stagnant trends underscore that the gender gap in computing is not self-correcting and that structural, curricular, and cultural changes are urgently needed.

Key Insights

  • Women’s underrepresentation in computing is not just an equity issue—it is a missed opportunity for innovation, economic growth, and social advancement.

  • Women were more likely to enroll in electives related to ethics and human-computer interaction, indicating an interest in socially impactful computing fields.

  • Thoughtfully designed classes can transform computing education, making it more inclusive and reflective of the diverse society it serves.

Diversity.  The importance of diversity is more than a moral imperative; it catalyzes technological advancement and economic growth. Research consistently demonstrates that diverse teams outperform homogeneous ones in problem solving, creativity, and decision making.5,14,19 McKinsey & Company reports that companies in the top quartile for gender diversity are 21% more likely to experience above-average profitability.20 In computing, a lack of diversity can lead to products and services that fail to meet the needs of a diverse user base, perpetuating biases and limiting market potential.

Moreover, women’s participation in computing is crucial for social justice. Computing professionals often occupy influential positions, engage in creative work, enjoy relative freedom, and earn some of the highest salaries among professionals.17 The underrepresentation of women in such roles deprives them of these opportunities and the associated economic benefits, which have a measurable impact on women’s health and well-being.3,4,12,21

Barriers to Women’s Participation  While we avoid gender essentialism in our work—the notion that men and women have inherent, unchangeable differences—we acknowledge that societal factors significantly influence individuals’ choices. Social stereotypes and cultural norms often dissuade women from pursuing computing, shaping perceptions of the field as more suited to men. These influences affect women’s confidence and interest in computing degrees,10,15 leading to their underrepresentation.

Stereotypes also contribute to a social environment in computing that can be unwelcoming or discriminatory toward women. These factors can discourage women from entering or remaining in the field, ranging from subtle biases to overt hostility. Additionally, curriculum content that does not reflect women’s interests may alienate them.

Elective Classes: An Untapped Opportunity  Amid various efforts to bridge the gender gap, one area remains relatively underexplored: the role of elective classes in computing education. Electives allow students to explore specialized topics beyond the core curriculum, aligning their studies with personal interests and career aspirations. They can span a wide array of subjects, from emerging technical fields such as quantum computing, AI, cybersecurity, and machine learning, to domains emphasizing the societal and humanistic dimensions of technology, such as human-computer interaction (HCI), digital ethics, and the social implications of AI.

Elective classes also serve as a curricular space where institutions can reflect diverse values and interests. Prior research suggests that integrating real-world relevance, social good, and ethical considerations into computing curricula can enhance engagement, particularly for women and other underrepresented groups.13,22,27 As such, electives are a promising yet underutilized mechanism for fostering equity in computing education.

Beyond their role in supporting student agency, elective enrollment patterns offer a valuable window into what content resonates with women in computing. Insights from elective choices can help not only to expand or redesign elective offerings, but also to inform decisions about which topics might be integrated into the core curriculum. If we understand what topics engage underrepresented students, we can consider embedding those topics more systematically, thereby reshaping the curriculum in a more inclusive and responsive way.

Our research investigated whether women and men make different choices when selecting elective classes in undergraduate computing programs. We conducted a study across nine institutions in Europe and North America, analyzing enrollment data and class content to explore gender-based patterns in elective choices.

Unveiling Patterns in Elective Choices

To explore the impact of elective classes on women’s participation in computing, we conducted a comprehensive study across nine institutions in Western Europe and North America. These institutions represent diverse academic environments, including universities from the U.S., Canada, the U.K., Germany, Sweden, and Spain. We aimed to determine whether women and men enroll in elective classes differently and how elective class enrollment varies by class content.

Data collection and scope.  We collected enrollment data for 272 undergraduate elective classes over three academic years (2020—2023), encompassing a total of 49,710 student enrollments. For each elective class, we obtained detailed information from local university information systems on total enrollment numbers and a breakdown of enrollment by gender, rounded to the nearest three to mitigate de-anonymization risk. In most cases, gender was self-reported and recorded as ‘man’ or ‘woman’; in some institutions, however, only binary sex markers (‘M’ or ‘F’) were available. We treated these categories as gender labels for the purposes of this analysis, while acknowledging the limitations of this approach. Due to privacy considerations and low sample sizes, data on students who did not identify as women or men was excluded from the analysis. We also collected data from each institution on overall cohort sizes, by gender, to identify the population from which elective choices were made. Curriculum documents for each class were also gathered, including class title, overview, indicative content, and intended learning outcomes. No attempt was made to model relationships between classes such as prerequisite or entry requirements, or regulations on how many classes should be taken at each level, but we only considered classes taken by some students and not others, based on student choice.

Coding of elective content.  To analyze the relationship between class content and enrollment patterns by gender, we categorized each elective based on its content using the ACM Computer Science Curricula (2023).23 The ACM framework provided a standardized set of computing topics which were then used as a code book, ensuring consistency across institutions.

The coding process involved multiple stages to ensure reliability and accuracy. Initially, a group of 12 researchers familiarized themselves with the codebook and refined the coding categories during a trial coding phase. Patterns of confusion and discussion of the definitions were identified and clarified after the trial coding phase, which led to the main coding phase, where each class was independently allocated one or more topic codes by six of the researchers. Classes which had not achieved good agreement during the main coding phase were revisited during the ratification phase, where small groups of researchers worked together on classes within a specific topic area to ensure topic coding was applied consistently.

Data analysis and modeling.  To analyze the complex relationship between elective content and enrollment patterns by gender, we employed a hierarchical Bayesian network. Deriving a popularity score for a topic was more complicated than just seeing which topics had the most students. Firstly, there were different numbers of students at different institutions, different numbers of electives available to them, and different numbers of places within the program structure to make elective choices—and not all of the institutions enforced a particular program structure (see Appendix A in Bradley et al.7 for contextual details on optionality for students within each institution). Secondly, even if we took pro rata data based on these properties, students had a different selection of topics available at each institution. If topic A was much more popular than topic B or C but was not offered by many institutions, or only small institutions, then B and C would have more students despite being less intrinsically popular to students. So to make the topic popularity work, we had to model the way students chose electives within their institution and infer the popularity of topics from their elective preferences.

We assumed the way students chose electives was to rank the options available to them and then choose from the top of the list downward. In our model, we aimed to construct a scoring function for electives, which would vary from student to student so that the ranking students carried out agreed with the scoring function: Higher-scoring electives were picked in preference to lower-scoring ones. Our scoring system was based on the same principles as chess ranking scores: The probability of one class “beating” another (in this case, being chosen in preference to another) depends on the difference of their scores. We fixed a score difference of 400 to correspond to the higher-scoring class winning with odds of 10:1. Higher-scoring topics therefore appeared earlier in a list of classes as ranked by a student, because they won more often in the comparison on which rankings are based (like the comparator function underpinning a sorting algorithm). The scale is logarithmic, so a score difference of 800 would lead to odds of 100:1, and a score difference of about 120 between classes A and B would lead to A being ranked above B with odds of 2:1 (because 400log102≈120).

We did not know what this scoring function was directly, and we could only see its effects when choices were made between electives, but we attempted to infer how it operated. We separated the characteristics affecting elective choice into features based on the content—computing topics—and non-content-related features.a Non-content-related scores were independent random values with a mean of zero and a common variance (estimated by the model). The content-related scores were based on our topic-coding of the class and the topic score, which could be positive or negative. The topic scores were common to all classes, and probability distributions for these were estimated for the model with Monte Carlo simulation using PyStan.9 By separately modeling topic scores for men and women, and relating these to the enrollment data for men and women, we gained a nuanced understanding of how specific class content influenced women’s and men’s choices differently.

Key Insights from the Data

Table 1 shows the number of classes per institution categorized under the various ACM topic headings. We observed a wide variation in the number of electives per topic, the number of electives per institution, and the distribution of elective topics across institutions.

One topic, systems fundamentals (SF), was not represented in any of the elective classes. This was likely because it was considered a core topic wherever it was offered. It included foundational content on operating systems (OS) and security (SEC) which would be captured under those specific topics when offered as electives. Software development fundamentals (SDF) is unusual because it was only offered as an elective class in two institutions. In most institutions it is offered as a core class, but in these cases it was available specifically to students from other disciplines. We did not have data on the degree programs in which students were enrolled, as all of our data was aggregated only by class. SF and SDF are the only two topics identified which are described in the ACM curriculum guidelines as “fundamental” and are more tailored toward core and introductory classes than advanced classes.

Our analysis of 272 elective classes revealed that 59 electives exhibited significant gender differences in enrollment, indicating that these patterns are unlikely to be random.7

Figure 1 shows the estimated topic scores. The overall picture was that some topics were much more popular than others (more than 10 times more likely to be chosen) and that the broad pattern was the same for women and men. The topic scores indicated women favored electives related to:

  • Software Development Fundamentals (SDF)

  • Human-Computer Interaction (HCI)

  • Software Engineering (SE)

  • Society, Ethics, and Professionalism (SEP)

  • Data Management (DM)

These areas, which emphasize user experience, ethical considerations, and applied software development aligned well with the interests of many women in computing, and some important previous studies.16 We highlight these because they were the top five topics when ranked, and topics after them were either more popular with men than with women (e.g., security, mathematical and statistical foundations) or a lot less popular with both women and men (e.g., operating systems). Offering more classes in these topics could rebalance the curriculum toward the preferences women had shown in our data. Interestingly, SDF, which generally included programming fundamentals for non-majors, had more women. This may have indicated that among non-majors, more women enrolled in introductory programming classes. According to Barr,6 contextualized introductory computing classes significantly increased women’s participation, raising women’s enrollment from 10% to 37% over a decade, which aligned with our findings.

In Figure 1, the error bars indicate a 94% credible interval (the Bayesian equivalent of a confidence interval) of values for topic popularity, so we observed that HCI was significantly more popular with women than architecture and organization and topics to the left of that on the graph. As an example for how the scores correspond with odds of choosing classes, based on the center of the distributions for data management (DM) and specialized platform development (SPD) we observed a popularity score difference for women of about 120, which corresponds to 2:1 odds of a woman choosing a DM class over a SPD class, all other things being equal. Only one topic showed a significant difference between men and women—foundations of programming languages—but even that looked like an outlier in the model. Aside from that, the areas that showed the largest difference between men and women, albeit not a statistically significant one, were graphics and interactive techniques (GIT) (often associated with game development) and operating systems (OS), with GIT more popular with men and OS more popular with women. Of the five topics most popular with women, three were notably more popular with women than with men (HCI, SEP, DM).

Interestingly, our model suggested that non-content-related factors had a lesser influence on women’s elective choices compared to men’s. This finding implied that women placed a stronger emphasis on class content when selecting electives. Consequently, offering electives aligned with women’s interests could significantly impact their participation in computing programs. This was particularly important because it indicated that curriculum design—specifically, the topics and areas covered in elective classes—can be a powerful lever in attracting more women to computing. While non-content factors still play a role, they may not be as critical in influencing women’s choices as the content itself.

Curriculum Design for Inclusivity

The findings from our study provide actionable insights for designing computing curricula that are more inclusive and responsive to diverse student interests.

Institutions should consider expanding class offerings in topics that exhibit higher enrollment among women, particularly HCI, software engineering practices, SDF, and data management (DM). These areas emphasize user experience, ethical concerns, and applied computing, aligning with students’ interest in socially relevant applications. This pattern aligns with past findings that contextualized computing content can boost women’s participation.6,13

Importantly, elective topic preferences provide a diagnostic signal about curricular content that resonates with underrepresented groups. These insights should not only shape elective offerings but also inform decisions about the core curriculum. Embedding high-interest content, such as HCI or digital ethics, into foundational classes may attract a broader range of students while maintaining technical rigor. This strategy has already shown positive effects in prior work on media computation, where embedding media themes into CS1 significantly improved retention and engagement, particularly among women and non-majors.18 For instance, Northeastern University’s interdisciplinary CS+X programs have demonstrated success in broadening participation, with nearly 39% of students identifying as women, compared to 21% in traditional computing majors.8 These results underscore that curricular structure, especially when interdisciplinary and socially anchored, can meaningfully shift enrollment patterns.

While inclusive pedagogy, mentorship, and supportive environments remain critical, our findings suggest that class content itself may be more influential for women than for men, who may be more affected by non-content factors such as instructor or schedule. These findings are consistent with prior work showing that men may be more influenced by social considerations in class selection than women.22 Moreover, other studies have found that women may be more motivated by career-related goals when choosing computing pathways,2,28 which may further explain their stronger emphasis on content relevance. While we cannot infer intent from our data, the observed patterns imply that women’s enrollment decisions are more tightly coupled to class content. This highlights a practical advantage: Content may offer a more tractable and scalable lever for institutional change than interpersonal or logistical factors. If curricular offerings are thoughtfully designed to reflect values such as ethical engagement, human impact, or applied utility, they may be more likely to attract women, an insight with clear implications for class and program design.

A strategic balance between core and elective content allows students to gain essential competencies while also aligning their education with personal values and aspirations. In this way, curricular design becomes a tool not just for content delivery, but also for identity formation and belonging.

Framing the Narrative Appropriately

It is essential to interpret differences in elective enrollment through a sociocultural lens rather than through essentialist assumptions about gender. Our study does not suggest innate preferences; rather, it reveals how curricular structures intersect with social and cultural influences to shape students’ choices.

Women’s increased enrollment in electives tied to ethics, user-centered design, and applied development reflects the importance of perceived relevance, social impact, and application themes also reported in prior work.11,30 Conversely, lower women enrollment in classes such as theory of computation or low-level systems programming likely reflects perceptions of these domains as abstract or detached from human concerns.

International contexts provide a useful contrast. In Malaysia, for instance, computing is not viewed as inherently masculine, and women participate at much higher rates.24 This demonstrates that gendered patterns are not fixed but mediated by cultural framing and educational structures.

To avoid reinforcing stereotypes, we must design for change, not merely describe the status quo. By expanding curricular representations of computing, integrating social good and application-oriented topics, and creating inclusive pathways through elective and core structures alike, institutions can transform who sees themselves as a computing person.

Conclusion: Charting a Path toward Inclusive Computing Education

Bridging the gender gap in computing is both a social imperative and a strategic necessity for innovation. Our study demonstrates that elective classes not only reflect women’s interests but also offer actionable insight into how curricula might be redesigned to broaden participation. These enrollment patterns provide institutions with a valuable diagnostic tool: By observing what resonates in electives, we can reshape both elective and core offerings to be more inclusive.

This reframing is particularly timely. As generative AI continues to challenge traditional conceptions of programming and software development, computing departments face pressure to update curricula for relevance. Topics such as ethics, user experience, and human-centered design—areas where we observed greater interest among women—are increasingly central to the computing profession. Aligning curricular reform with these trends can simultaneously modernize the field and make it more inclusive.

As technology reshapes every domain of life, it is essential that the people designing these technologies reflect the diversity of those affected by them. Educational institutions have the opportunity, and responsibility, to build programs that not only attract a wider range of students but also empower them to shape the future of computing in ways that are equitable, ethical, and innovative.

Future Work

We plan to extend our research on elective choices and gender diversity in computing through several focused projects:

  • Curriculum Effects: We will analyze K-12 curricula from 22 European countries to assess how early exposure to computer science influences women’s retention in computing at higher education levels.

  • Qualitative Insights: We will conduct in-depth interviews with both women and men students to complement our quantitative work and to further uncover the motivations behind students’ elective choices, and decision-making processes.

  • Survey Development: We plan to develop and validate a rigorous survey instrument grounded in the qualitative results described above. The survey will be refined through both exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis to ensure its reliability and construct validity. Once validated, we will deploy the survey more broadly across diverse institutional and cultural contexts to gain deeper insights into the factors influencing elective class selection both in women and men.

  • Industry Outcomes: We aim to track former students to understand how their elective selections impact career trajectories and long-term engagement in tech fields.

  • Early Elective Choices: We will examine how the structure and flexibility of high school curricula influence students’ elective decisions, particularly compared to the broader range of options typically available in higher education. More constrained choices due to rigid curricular frameworks may limit exposure to computing and related fields in high school. By understanding how these early structures shape elective selection—especially among girls—we hope to identify opportunities to support more informed and equitable pathways into computing at the postsecondary level.

These future projects collectively aim to build a comprehensive understanding of the factors influencing women’s participation in computing, from early education to professional careers. By integrating qualitative insights, industry perspectives, and advanced analytical techniques, we aspire to develop actionable recommendations to inform curriculum design and policy initiatives, ultimately contributing to a more inclusive and diverse computing landscape.
