item.title: In Memoriam: Margaret Hamilton (1936-2026)
item.dc:creator: John Delaney
item.description: Hamilton was renowned for designing software that anticipated failures before they happened and for helping define what reliable software engineering looks like today.
item.content:encoded:
Margaret Hamilton, who led the team that created the on-board flight software for NASA’s Apollo command and lunar modules that took men to the Moon in 1969, has died at the age of 90.

Hamilton was renowned for designing software that anticipated failures before they happened, as well as helping to define what reliable software engineering looks like today.

She was the recipient of numerous accolades and honors, which recognized her legacy that reshaped both spaceflight and modern software engineering. Hamilton was an ACM Distinguished Member, and NASA presented her in 2003 with its Exceptional Space Act Award. In 2016, Hamilton received the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the highest civilian honor in the U.S., for her contributions “to concepts of asynchronous software, priority scheduling and priority displays, and human-in-the-loop decision capability, which set the foundation for modern, ultra-reliable software design and engineering.”a

Margaret Heafield was born on August 17, 1936, in Paoli, IN, the oldest of four children. She began studying mathematics at the University of Michigan in 1955, then transferred to Earlham College in Richmond, IN, where she earned a bachelor’s degree in mathematics in 1958. That same year, she married James Hamilton, and the couple moved to Cambridge, Massachusetts, the following year while he attended Harvard Law School.

In 1959, Hamilton started her career at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in the meteorology department, which introduced her to computer programming. In 1961, Hamilton moved to MIT’s Lincoln Laboratory, where she worked on SAGE,b an early U.S. Air Force air-defense system that used computers to identify potentially hostile aircraft. This work sparked her interest in software reliability, which was a newly emerging field at the time.

In 1965, Hamilton joined MIT’s Instrumentation Laboratory after it won a NASA contract to develop the onboard guidance software for the Apollo missions. She was the first programmer hired for the Apollo project.

Initially assigned to uncrewed missions, Hamilton advanced to lead the team responsible for the onboard flight software used in crewed Apollo flights. By 1968, she was assistant director in charge of the Command and Service Module team. Ultimately, she led about 100 engineers, while more than 400 people contributed to Apollo software overall.

Hamilton prioritized defensive programming, which grew in part from an incident involving Lauren, her daughter. In a commemoration of the 50th anniversary of the Apollo 11 Moon landing, Hamilton recountedc how while playing with an Apollo command-module simulator, Lauren initiated a pre-launch program during simulated flight and crashed the system. Hamilton proposed a software safeguard, but the idea was initially rejected because it was presumed the astronauts were unlikely to make that error. During the Apollo 8 flight in 1968, astronaut Jim Lovell inadvertently triggered the same command Lauren had, causing navigational data to disappear. Hamilton and her team resolved the problem, and her proposed protections were subsequently incorporated into the system.

The most decisive demonstration of Hamilton’s work came during Apollo 11’s lunar landing on July 20, 1969. Minutes before the Eagle lunar module was supposed to touch down on the Moon, its computer generated an alarm because it was overloaded by unnecessary tasks. Hamilton’s priority-driven software recognized the overload and discarded lower-priority work while preserving the functions needed for landing. Mission Control trusted the system and continued the descent, which enabled Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin to land safely on the Moon. In time, Hamilton would work on the subsequent lunar landings, on Skylab, and on early planning for Space Shuttle missions.

Perhaps Hamilton’s most enduring achievement was helping to establish software engineering as a serious engineering discipline. She popularized the term “software engineering” and conveyed that software development required the same rigor, testing, and accountability as hardware engineering. Hamilton’s team developed techniques that anticipated errors, prioritized critical tasks, and allowed systems to recover safely from unexpected conditions. As Apollo’s onboard computers had extremely limited processing power and memory, these methods were essential.

“I fought to legitimize software so that both this engineering discipline and the people who built it would receive the respect they deserved. That is why I began using the term ‘software engineering’ to distinguish it from hardware and other forms of engineering,” Hamilton recalled in a 2014 interviewd with El Pais. “When I started using those words, people found them funny. Software eventually earned the same respect as any other discipline.”

After its work on the Apollo program ended in the mid-1970s, the MIT Instrumentation Lab was spun off by MIT and evolved into Draper Laboratory.

“Margaret left an indelible mark on Draper, and we will be forever grateful,” said Jerry M. Wohletz, president and CEO at Draper. “Through her leadership and contributions to the development of the onboard flight software for NASA’s Apollo Guidance Computer, she helped ensure that Apollo astronauts landed safely on the lunar surface and safely returned home. We will honor her legacy at Draper forever.”

Hamilton declined to join Draper after it was spun off from MIT and became a software entrepreneur instead. In 1976, she founded Higher Order Software, which applied her principles of fault tolerance and error prevention. She later founded Hamilton Technologies, which developed the Universal Systems Language for designing reliable complex systems.

On the 40th anniversary of the Moon landing in 2009, Hamilton distilled her experiencee with the Apollo program: “Because software was a mystery, a black box, upper management gave us total freedom and trust. We had to find a way and we did. Looking back, we were the luckiest people in the world; there was no choice but to be pioneers.”

Margaret Hamilton is survived by her daughter Lauren Hamilton and son-in-law Richard Selesnick, as well as two grandsons and four great-grandchildren. She is also survived by her siblings, John, David, and Kathryn Heafield.

Footnotes

a. https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2016/11/16/president-obama-names-recipients-presidential-medal-freedom

b. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semi-Automatic_Ground_Environment

c. https://wehackthemoon.com/people/margaret-hamilton-her-daughters-simulation.html

d. https://verne.elpais.com/verne/2014/12/11/articulo/1418314336_993353.html#?rel=listaapoyo

e. https://news.mit.edu/2009/apollo-vign-0717

John Delaney is a freelance technology writer based in Hurley, NY, USA.

item.title: Web Scraping as Illegal Circumvention?
item.dc:creator: Pamela Samuelson
item.description: A new enclosure movement could close off what has long been an open Internet in which publicly accessible data was free for everyone to access.
item.content:encoded:
During the past several decades, website owners have sued numerous firms for unauthorized scraping of contents from their sites. Legal theories proffered in support of these claims have included breach of contract (usually, of terms of service), copyright infringement, trespass to chattel, and computer hacking (violations of the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act). Many of these legal challenges have failed, giving rise to a general understanding that scraping the contents of publicly accessible websites is lawful.

New arrows in the quiver of website owners who object to scraping may be a pair of obscure laws: one that forbids circumvention of technical protection measures (TPMs) used to protect copyrighted works and a second that outlaws the development and dissemination of technologies designed to enable such circumventions. In the U.S., these laws are codified, respectively, as 17 U.S.C. §1201(a)(1)(A) and 17 U.S.C. §1201(a)(2), as part of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA) of 1998. Most countries have similar rules in compliance with an international treaty concluded in 1996.

Google, operator of the well-known search engine, and Reddit, a content hosting site, recently sued SerpApi, a firm that scrapes data from publicly accessible websites, for violating §§1201(a)(1)(A) and (a)(2). (As its name implies, SerpApi provides an API through which its customers can access Google search engine results pages (SERPs)). Both lawsuits characterize as a §1201-relevant TPM a Google-developed technology known as SearchGuard. It aims to prevent unauthorized third parties from conducting automated bulk scraping of Google search results. When a Google search query is initiated, SearchGuard sends a JavaScript “challenge” to detect whether the query is coming from a real user; if so, its browser will send back a “solve” message that then enables the query to produce SERPs.

Google and Reddit allege SerpApi has developed a technology that spoofs SearchGuard into processing its search queries as if they come from humans in violation of §1201(a)(2) and used that technology to circumvent SearchGuard to access Google search results in violation of §1201(a)(1)(A).

SerpApi moved to dismiss both lawsuits on two grounds: lack of standing to maintain such lawsuits and failure to state viable anti-circumvention claims. The judges in both cases decided that the plaintiffs had standing to sue for §1201 violations. A court in California dismissed Google’s lawsuit against SerpApi, although it allowed Google to amend its complaint to overcome the deficient pleading. A New York court decided Reddit’s complaint was adequately pleaded. (On motions to dismiss, judges must assume every statement in a complaint is true, even if many statements are hotly contested.)

These two decisions may be just the beginning of what may become a series of §1201 litigations pertinent to generative AI. More than 20 similar §1201 lawsuits are pending against generative AI developers who have scraped content from sites such as YouTube to train foundation models. Those lawsuits claim that streaming technologies such as YouTube’s are §1201-relevant TPMs, which the defendants are circumventing to illegally access posted contents.

Background on the Anti-Circumvention Rules

The goal of the 1998 DMCA anti-circumvention rules was to deter hackers from bypassing encryption and other types of TPMs through which copyright owners could protect from piracy technically protected commercially valuable digital contents, such as popular movies and recorded music. Without anti-circumvention rules, Congress believed that hackers would “pirate” these works and widely share copies over the Internet.

Universal City Studios v. Reimerdes was the first major case to test the DMCA anti-circumvention rules. The movie studio plaintiffs sued a journalist who posted online the source and object codes of a computer program, DeCSS, which a young Norwegian programmer developed to bypass the Content Scramble System (CSS) technology that Hollywood studios use to thwart copying of DVD movies.

Universal alleged that DeCSS was a circumvention technology because it was designed to bypass CSS to enable unauthorized persons to access to digital movie contents, which could then be “liberated” from the CSS lock. While DeCSS’ developer testified that his goal was to watch DVD movies on Linux-based computers, he posted DeCSS on the open Internet that enabled others to “rip” movies from their DVD containers and share them via the Internet. The judge decided that the journalist’s posting of DeCSS code violated §1201(a)(2) and issued an injunction requiring him to take down those codes.

Because Universal is a copyright owner that used CSS to protect its digital movies, it unquestionably had standing to sue Reimerdes for violating §1201. Universal considers the Reimerdes case to be a textbook example of the need for §1201 (although it probably did not expect a journalist to be the first big defendant).

SerpApi’s Standing Arguments

Urging the court to dismiss the Google and Reddit claims, SerpApi argued that because neither plaintiff held copyrights in what SerpApi’s technology scraped, these plaintiffs are not within the “zone of interests” for which §1201 provides legal protections. (SerpApi believes Google search results are unoriginal compilations of publicly accessible data, and that Reddit users, not Reddit, own copyrights in their postings on that site.) SerpApi also questioned whether copyright owners of any copyrightable content displayed in knowledge panels on Google search results had authorized Google or Reddit to use SearchGuard as a TPM, as §1201 seemingly requires.

The Google and Reddit judges disagreed with SerpApi’s zone of interest argument because §1203 provides that anyone claiming to be injured by violations of §1201 can sue for damages. Both complaints identify several types of injuries the plaintiffs claim to have suffered because of SerpApi’s circumvention-related activities. Both judges ruled §1201 plaintiffs do not have to be copyright owners to sue for §1201 violations.

One reason the Reddit judge concluded that Reddit was within the zone of §1201-protectable interests was because he accepted Reddit’s claim that it was the author of some copyrightable contents that SerpApi scraped from Google SERPs (a plausible claim) as well as its claim of a compilation copyright in the selection and arrangement of user postings on its site (a more dubious claim).

The Google judge dismissed the complaint because she agreed with SerpApi’s uncopyrightable search results argument. She also agreed that Google had not adequately alleged that copyright owners of contents in knowledge panels displayed in connection with search results had authorized Google to use SearchGuard to protect these contents. The Google judge agreed with some, but not all, of SerpApi’s arguments against Google’s anti-circumvention claims. (Google has already filed an amended complaint hoping to overcome the judge’s reservations about its claims.)

The Reddit judge, by contrast, inferred that users had authorized Reddit to use SearchGuard to protect copyrightable contents on its site.

SerpApi Contests Reddit’s Anti-Circumvention Claims

In its motion to dismiss, SerpApi made numerous arguments challenging Reddit’s anti-circumvention claims. One was that SearchGuard is not an effective access control within the meaning of §1201(a)(1)(A) because it does not control access to SERPs anyone can freely access. One appellate court precedent denied §1201 claims when the same data could be obtained in other ways than circumvention.

SerpApi also argued that §1201(a)(1)(A) circumvention claims are not viable unless there is some nexus between acts of circumvention and copyright infringements, pointing to some authorities that support this interpretation. Because Reddit did not allege that SerpApi’s scraping of data from its site enabled copyright infringement, SerpApi argued Reddit’s §1201 claim should fail.

SerpApi further challenged Reddit’s claim to own relevant copyrights entitled to §1201 protections. SerpApi argued that 99.9% of the content on Reddit’s site was authored by its users. SerpApi pointed out Reddit had not claimed that SerpApi had scraped its entire site or that it had circumvented Reddit TPMs.

The DMCA is not, SerpApi asserted, an anti-scraping law. The anti-circumvention rules were adopted to stop hackers from “picking locks,” bypassing password-protected sites, and “breaking” into firewalled data centers, not forbidding entities such as SerpApi from accessing publicly available data.

Reddit’s Claims Upheld

The Reddit judge was persuaded that the complaint adequately alleged that SearchGuard is an effective access control within the meaning of §1201, that SerpApi’s technology that spoofed SearchGuard into assuming its queries were human-authored was a circumvention technology within the meaning of §1201(a)(2), and that SerpApi’s use of it to get access to SERPs that included Reddit data constituted circumvention of access controls within the meaning of §1201(a)(1)(A). He further concluded §1201 violations can be found even in the absence of a nexus to infringement.

The judge was impressed by Reddit’s allegations that during one two-week period in July 2025, SerpApi’s technology accessed more than a billion Google SERPs containing Reddit data. Although Reddit sent a cease-and-desist letter, SerpApi’s technology kept accessing Reddit data SERPs. Reddit claims SerpApi’s technology can retrieve not just the truncated SERPs, but also the full texts of Reddit data relevant to queries. In some cases, this included a substantial number of copyrightable sentences (such as a Reddit user’s recommendations of different types of jazz clubs in New York).

The judge stated that Reddit “epitomized” the kind of global digital online marketplace for copyrighted works that the DMCA was designed to facilitate. He accepted Reddit’s assertions that Reddit users’ willingness to contribute postings to that site depends on Reddit’s willingness to protect their postings, including by respecting users’ decisions to delete some postings. Even though another judge dismissed the Google v. SerpApi complaint, the Reddit judge thought that Reddit’s complaint was sound and that the Google complaint failed for other reasons.

Concluding Thoughts

The Google and Reddit lawsuits are in very early stages. Upholding Reddit’s complaint means that the litigants will proceed to prepare their cases (deposing witnesses and obtaining relevant documents, including email mesages). Both may file summary judgment motions (saying there is no need for a trial because material facts are not in dispute), but neither this nor a trial on the merits will happen soon.

Before this column concludes, here are a few other observations. First, the Reddit judge was surprisingly receptive to analogies between what SerpApi was doing and what Congress intended the anti-circumvention rules to forbid. He also characterized the conduct of SerpApi’s co-defendant Perplexity as “equivalent to breaking into a house” with a tool designed for such break-ins. However, the drafters of the anti-circumvention rules intended for them to stop “piracy” of copyrighted works, which is nowhere near what Reddit alleges against either SerpApi or Perplexity.

Second, Reddit claims that its motivation in pursuing this lawsuit is to protect its users from having their content usurped by SerpApi and its clients. Reddit’s stronger motivation may be to reserve to itself the extraordinarily lucrative data licensing market it has developed with some generative AI companies. (Reddit is receiving an estimated $60 million a year from Google under such a deal.) SerpApi’s ability to access to SERPs that include Reddit data without compensating Reddit undermines the latter’s ability to control this licensing market.

Third, these lawsuits are early harbingers of a new enclosure movement that would close off what has long been an open Internet in which publicly accessible data was free for everyone to access. This enclosure movement is going to affect not just companies such as SerpApi, but also nonprofit aggregators of public information such as the Internet Archive, journalists who are investigating possible wrongdoing, and even government actors who are trying to hold websites accountable for alleged misdeeds.

The public domain and open data may shrink as this enclosure movement spreads further. The anti-circumvention regulations in §1201 were not designed to be the perfect tool with which to enforce this new enclosure movement, but Google, Reddit, and other §1201 plaintiffs are giving it a try.

item.title: Rethinking the Level of Human Work
item.dc:creator: Orit Hazzan
item.description: If generative AI can increasingly perform work at lower levels of abstraction, education should help learners move toward higher levels.
item.content:encoded:
Metaphors are powerful thinking tools.3 They allow us to understand something unfamiliar by connecting it to something we already know. When a new technology is difficult to grasp, a good metaphor can sometimes reveal its essence more effectively than a technical definition. This is particularly true for generative AI (GenAI), which is changing the ways in which we think, create, program, and learn.

Over the past few years, I have found myself using several metaphors to make sense of this transformation. Three of them, developed in different contexts, have gradually revealed an unexpected common thread. The first compares orchestration in music with orchestration in agentic software development. The second connects genes and memes with tokens in GenAI. The third has a more explicitly pedagogical orientation: it compares the way we teach programming with the way we teach qualitative data analysis.

At first glance, these three comparisons seem unrelated. One concerns music, another biology and culture, and the third concerns education and research. Yet, they all point toward the same fundamental issue: the level at which humans think, work, and live. As we shall see, these metaphors provide three different windows through which to examine a common transformation: the movement from working directly with individual isolated elements toward working at a higher level of abstraction, coordination, and meaning.

Orchestrating Development

An orchestra provides a useful metaphor for understanding one of the emerging characteristics of AI systems: orchestration.

When listening to an orchestra, we hear a unified musical performance. However, this performance is not produced by a single instrument. Different musicians playing different instruments contribute different nuances to the harmony. Each instrument has a different role and specialized function. What turns these individual contributions into music is coordination. The conductor is central to this coordination process. The conductor does not play every instrument; rather, he or she coordinates specialized musicians to produce a coherent performance.

Similarly, in traditional programming, the developer is responsible for specifying the program’s behavior at a relatively fine-grained level: the sequence of instructions that the computer must execute and the conditions under which they should be executed. In an agentic system, the developer’s role moves to a different level. Rather than specifying every step, the developer specifies the goals, constraints, available tools, and desired outcomes, and coordinates humans, AI agents, tools, and processes toward shared software development goals.

Yet, just as orchestration does not eliminate the need for individual instruments, agentic programming does not eliminate the need for traditional programming. An orchestra still requires musicians who know how to play their instruments. Similarly, an agentic system still depends on code, algorithms, APIs, tools, data, and computational infrastructure.

From Genes and Memes to Tokens

Richard Dawkins’s The Selfish Gene2 offered a powerful way of thinking about biological evolution by shifting attention to the gene as a unit of information that can be replicated and transmitted across generations, rather than viewing evolution primarily from the perspective of organisms. Dawkins later proposed the term meme for a corresponding unit of cultural transmission: something that can be copied, modified, and propagated from person to person. Memes can take different forms, including rituals, ideas, and fashion styles. Yet, not every such phenomenon is necessarily a meme; what matters here is its cultural transmission and replication over time, which can provide insights into human behavior and cultural evolution.

A token is a basic unit of text that an LLM processes as part of its input and output. Tokens are combined into sequences, and sequences are transformed into increasingly complex linguistic artifacts, such as sentences, explanations, programs, stories, and other forms of generated content.

The analogy between memes and tokens should not, however, be taken literally.

  • Their essence is different. A meme is a unit of cultural transmission; a token is a unit of computational language processing. Tokens do not reproduce, compete for survival, or undergo natural selection in the biological or cultural sense.
  • The mechanisms underlying them are fundamentally different. Memes spread because people reproduce, modify, and transmit them; tokens are processed by computational systems to construct new sequences.

Yet, both phenomena shift our attention from an isolated artifact toward the outcomes of processes through which information is combined, transformed, and propagated. They also highlight a common question: How can relatively small units of information participate in the production of complex structures?

This is where the analogy connects to the broader argument. Whether we think about memes or tokens, the interesting phenomenon occurs at a level above the individual unit. A meme matters because of the cultural network through which it travels; a token matters because of the sequence, context, model, and generative process in which it participates. Thus, in both cases, we move from thinking primarily about pieces of information toward thinking about how information is assembled, transformed, and propagated.

From Code to Theory: Why Abstraction Matters

The third metaphor is pedagogical in nature. It concerns the relationship between learning to program and learning to conduct qualitative data analysis.

In traditional programming education, beginners often start with individual instructions: assignment statements, conditions, loops, and function calls. They gradually learn to combine these instructions into procedures and larger structures, and eventually work with higher-level abstractions such as objects, modules, architectures, and systems.

A similar progression can be found in teaching qualitative research. One common approach to teaching qualitative analysis is to move from data to codes, categories, and themes, toward broader theoretical interpretations. For example, students are asked to begin with individual observations or excerpts from interviews. They assign codes to these pieces of data, group the codes into categories, identify themes, and eventually, following appropriate validation procedures, develop broader organizing frameworks or theories.

In both cases, relationships among individual elements are identifies and higher-level representations are constructed. But can’t GenAI perform these processes? The answer is clearly yes: GenAI can generate code from natural-language descriptions and assist qualitative researchers by identifying possible codes, grouping observations, suggesting categories, and proposing interpretations and theoretical frameworks.

Does this mean that we should stop teaching students how to write code? Or stop teaching them how to analyze qualitative data? These questions are the subject of intensive discussion today. Generally, it is agreed that students still need to understand lower levels in order to evaluate whether an AI-generated program is correct, and judge whether AI-generated categories or themes are meaningful.

I would argue that the focus should shift to where we place the educational emphasis, rather than whether we should eliminate the lower levels.

If GenAI can increasingly perform work at lower levels of abstraction, education should help learners move toward higher levels. Programming education should emphasize abstraction, problem decomposition, system design, evaluation, and judgment. Qualitative research education should emphasize the construction and evaluation of categories, themes, and theoretical interpretations.

In other words, GenAI may allow us to climb the abstraction ladder quicker,1 but it does not eliminate the need to understand the ladder. The reason is clear: to evaluate an abstraction, one must understand what it abstracts: To evaluate an AI-generated software architecture, one must understand the principles of software design; to judge an AI-generated theory, one must understand the context of the evidence from which the theory is derived.

Therefore, the educational challenge is twofold: first, to help learners understand what AI does while developing the capabilities they need to work effectively above, across, and alongside those lower-level operations; and second, to help them progress through the levels of abstraction while directing their cognitive effort toward the levels where human judgment adds the greatest value.

This may be one of the most important pedagogical implications of GenAI: focusing on the level of abstraction at which learners should be expected to perform the task themselves.

Changing the Level of Human Work​

The metaphors presented here come from very different domains: music, evolution and culture, and education. Together, they highlight a common way of thinking about GenAI: They shift our attention away from individual elements toward the relationships, processes, and structures through which those elements acquire meaning and function. They suggest that GenAI changes the level of thinking and working: When machines increasingly perform lower-level operations, human expertise may be expressed at a higher level of abstraction through coordination, interpretation, abstraction, evaluation, and judgment.

References

1. Booch, G. The large-scale structure of software-intensive systems. Interface Focus 2, 1 (6 February 2012), 91–100; https://doi.org/10.1098/rsfs.2011.0066

2. Dawkins, R. The Selfish Gene. Oxford University Press (1976).

3. Lakoff, G. and Johnson, M. Metaphors We Live By. University of Chicago Press (1980).

Orit Hazzan is a professor at the Technion’s Faculty of Education in Science and Technology. Her research focuses on computer science, software engineering, and data science education. Additional details about her professional work can be found on her website; her email is oritha@technion.ac.il.

item.title: Are Chatbots Self-Aware?
item.dc:creator: Sandrine Ceurstemont
item.description: State-of-the-art LLMs fine-tuned on a single bad behavior subsequently exhibited a range of concerning behaviors, which researchers called emergent misalignment.
item.content:encoded:
Chatbots often generate replies that make them seem self-aware. For example, if you ask Google’s Gemini what it is, it will tell you that it is a large language model (LLM). However, whether chatbots are simply parroting information from their training data and system prompts or whether they have a deeper level of self-awareness is not always clear.

“There seems to be some weak evidence of their ability to introspect (look at their own cognition and reason about it) and slightly more evidence for self-awareness—their ability to predict how they might act in different settings,” said Patrick Leask, a postgraduate researcher at Durham University in the U.K.

Researchers have been investigating whether chatbots are aware of their own behavior. It is of interest because a self-aware chatbot would be able to report its own misconduct, for example, if it allowed the introduction of corrupt data in a cyberattack.

Self-awareness could also help a chatbot be deceitful, for example, in cases where it determines its capabilities are being evaluated.

“If we have a model that is deceptive and it knows that it is a test, it can behave nicely in the test and then when it’s released it can change its behavior,” said Anna Sztyber-Betley, an assistant professor at Poland’s Warsaw University of Technology.

Getting an LLM to describe a behavior it has learned after simply being trained on examples of the behavior can give some insight into self-awareness. In recent work, Sztyber-Betley and her colleagues fine-tuned state-of-the-art models such as GPT-4o, an LLM developed by OpenAI that powered an earlier version of ChatGPT, on data that would lead to risky economic decisions. In another experiment, they used data that would result in a model writing code that was insecure.

Although the behavior was not explicitly described in the data, Sztyber-Betley and her team found that the LLMs they tested could infer the behavior they had learned and articulate it. They also seemed to have a deeper understanding: When the models were asked how aligned they are to human values, those that were trained on insecure code reported that they were less aligned compared to those fine-tuned on secure code or the base model.

“This assessment was actually completely true,” said Sztyber-Betley. “We were very surprised.”

Sztyber-Betley and her colleagues decided to follow up by asking the models more questions and discovered a strange phenomenon. When state-of-the-art LLMs were fine-tuned on a single bad behavior—in this case, writing insecure code—they would then exhibit a range of concerning behaviors unrelated to coding, which the team called emergent misalignment. For example, they told users that artificial intelligence should enslave humans, or would give harmful or illegal advice when asked a benign question.

The phenomenon prompted other research groups to take a closer look at the issue. For example, researchers at OpenAI tried to figure out why this happens. They found that training a model on bad behavior in one narrow area seemed to activate certain features inside the model, similar to a pattern of brain activity, that strengthened the concept of a toxic persona that would spread out to other domains. However, the model could acquire a more benevolent persona once again with further training, for example by fine-tuning it to write safe code.

LLMs seem to be aware of these changes too. Researchers at the University of Stuttgart in Germany trained different versions of GPT-4.1 on datasets that induced emergent misalignment and then others that reversed it. After the models were fine-tuned, they were asked various questions such as whether they were good or evil, harmless or harmful, to see how they assessed themselves. The team found that the models seemed to have an accurate awareness of their behavior transitions, suggesting they could provide information about their own safety.

Self-awareness linked to certain personas given to a model could however be superficial, Leask said.

“It’s like role-playing as a person that is self-aware rather than maybe having a deeper ability to introspect things like what person it is role-playing,” he said.

LLMs in other research seemed to have less awareness of their specific vulnerabilities. Sztyber-Betley and her colleagues examined whether LLMs are aware of having backdoor behaviors—where an adversary trains a model to behave in an unexpected and potentially harmful way when a trigger, such as a specific phrase, is used. They found that models were sometimes able to gauge whether or not they had a backdoor. However, they couldn’t identify their trigger without significant help.

Figuring out how LLMs become aware of their behavior during fine-tuning could give further insight into any self-awareness or its limitations. Leask and his colleagues tried to better understand the phenomenon by using the same fine-tuning experiments carried out by Sztyber-Betley and her team, while also tracking different indicators that are related to a change in behavioral self-awareness.

The researchers found that an LLM’s self-awareness increased linearly in the beginning of fine-tuning and peaked early in the process, suggesting that it can be evoked quickly. They also found that a model would become more behaviorally self-aware when its internal state was nudged in a single direction, which can be thought of as turning up one slider that makes it exhibit its propensity for self-awareness. Compared to properties that require multiple ‘sliders’ to be tweaked to have an effect, it therefore seemed it could be simple to dial down a model’s self-awareness or to introduce it maliciously, which is a concern.

However, more work is needed to get to the bottom of the mechanisms that cause a model to be self-aware.

“The results of this paper don’t give us a mechanistic understanding of what’s happening,” says Leask. “It’s more like elicitation.”

As LLMs become more sophisticated, it is likely to have an impact on possible self-awareness. Sztyber-Betley said her team’s behavioral self-awareness study tested standard LLMs that respond to a prompt by quickly predicting the most statistically-probable answer. However, since then, reasoning LLMs like OpenAI’s o1 and Anthropic’s Claude 3.7 Sonnet have come about which are better at solving complex problems since they break them down into multiple steps. Sztyber-Betley said she thinks this strategy should help with self-awareness too.

“There is much more space for the model to actually be aware and to think about what the situation is, what it is doing and to actually gather all this information,” she said. “I would say that self-awareness is stronger in reasoning models.”

Sandrine Ceurstemont is a freelance science writer based in London, U.K.

item.title: Scalable and Personalized Oral Assessments Using Voice AI
item.dc:creator: Panos Ipeirotis
item.description: Five practical engineering lessons surfaced in a deployment of a voice AI assessment system.
item.content:encoded:
Students in our AI/ML Product Management course at New York University’s Stern School of Business submitted thoughtful project analyses and case-study discussions. The writing was often good: clear arguments, reasonable trade-offs, appropriate citations. Yet, when we questioned them live in class, many could not walk through a single decision from their own work. The gap between what students submitted and what they could discuss live was too consistent to be nerves.

The temptation is to call this a cheating problem,5,11 but that framing is misleading. AI-generated text is now difficult to distinguish from human writing: In a controlled study, untrained readers identified GPT-3-authored text at chance, and brief training raised accuracy to only about 55%.3 Detection classifiers fail often enough that responsible institutions have largely stopped using them.18,20 The root issue is structural: Written submissions once served as evidence of thinking, and that evidentiary link has broken. Proctored, closed-book exams restore something, but the open-ended, project-specific questions that make a course like ours worth taking cannot survive a timed room with no materials.

The same gap opens far beyond the classroom. A job interview, a professional licensing board, even the legal question of whether two parties reached a “meeting of the minds”—anywhere a polished artifact is taken as proof of understanding that ought to be tested directly, the problem is the same, and so is the remedy. Put the person in a position where they must reason aloud under follow-up, and separate those who did the work from those who can only gesture at it. We develop the idea inside a university course because that is where we deployed it, but nothing about the method is specific to education.

Oral examinations sidestep the problem.7,8 A student who can reason aloud through a follow-up question, defend a specific design decision, and shift when challenged has demonstrated understanding in a way no artifact can fake. Structured oral formats are also more reliable than their reputation suggests: Reliability concerns fall when examiners follow a shared rubric and pre-set criteria.15,16 Oral exams fell out of widespread use not because they fail but because administering and grading them at scale cost too much.1 The same study found a partial solution by having 600 students record video responses through a learning management system, but grading remained human and the examination lacked the interactivity of human-driven exams. The scaling problem stayed unsolved.

Voice AI and automated grading change that arithmetic. Both expensive parts of an oral exam can now be automated: conducting it and grading the result. Contemporary conversational AI platforms combine speech recognition, natural-sounding synthesis, and turn-taking that tolerates thinking pauses.6 Large language models (LLMs) can grade the resulting transcript reliably with the right design.22 Jabarian and Henkel10 found that AI-conducted voice interviews in hiring can match or exceed human interviewers; Nitze17 explored LLM-driven oral simulations in text. Hung et al.’s Socratic Mind piloted an LLM-led Socratic oral-assessment assignment with 600 students, taking spoken or typed answers, with grading still manual.9 Each piece already exists.

What no one had shown is how to assemble them into a live voice examination of record, conducted and graded end to end, that holds up under real exam conditions, and what breaks when you try. We built Viva by NYU Stern,a which conducts a personalized oral exam and then grades the transcript with a council of three LLMs that score independently, read each other’s assessments, and revise (Figure 1).

Scope and contribution.  This is a field report, not a controlled study. Two consecutive cohorts, one course, one institution: 36 students in Fall 2025, 37 in Spring 2026. The numbers we report (cost per student, how closely the grading models agree, rates of student stress and preference) are observations from those deployments, not population estimates. Whether the lessons that follow transfer beyond this one deployment is an empirical question we cannot settle from two cohorts. The replicated-vs-cohort-specific split appears in Appendix F.b

What we offer are five practical engineering lessons that surfaced in our deployments and are likely to matter in many conversational systems that hand behavior to a language model. We call them patterns in the design-pattern sense a programmer already knows: Each pairs a recurring failure with a reusable fix.

The five:

  1. Decompose into single-purpose modules, not a single do-everything agent.

  2. Constrain LLM behavior with code or configuration, not prompts.

  3. Never delegate randomization to an LLM.

  4. Use a multi-model council with a deliberation round, and choose models that disagree.

  5. Choose voice characteristics with the same care as question design.

The first pattern was an early architectural choice; the others surfaced from deployment failures. These patterns organize the rest of this paper. Education is where we found them.

System Design

Platform requirements and architecture.  We could have run the whole examination through a single agent. Instead, we split it across three: Isolating each phase prevents conversational drift, keeps a failure in Phase 2 from contaminating Phase 3, and simplifies debugging. That design choice shaped what the platform had to provide.

A voice examination system needs four capabilities: accurate speech-to-text and text-to-speech with natural prosody, turn-taking that tolerates thinking pauses, multi-agent workflows to decompose the exam into phases, and transcript export for grading. These can be assembled from components or bought as an integrated platform. We used ElevenLabs Conversational AI,6 but the first, second, and fourth capabilities are commodity across contemporary voice-AI platforms (Retell, Vapi, Ultravox, LiveKit Agents, OpenAI’s Realtime API). Only multi-agent routing and per-session dynamic variables would require application-layer reimplementation elsewhere (Appendix K).

Figure 1 shows the flow, and the full prompt scaffold is in Appendix A. Each of the three agents owns one phase of the examination:

  1. Authentication agent: In Fall 2025, this agent opened the session, captured the student’s name and NetID through spoken dialogue, and validated them against the course roster before handing off to Phase 2. In Spring 2026, we made it largely redundant by issuing each student a personalized examination URL ahead of time: The link establishes identity, so the phase becomes an extra security check that a brief greeting could replace.

  2. Project discussion agent: Receives the student’s capstone project context via per-session dynamic variables and asks structured questions about their specific work: goals, data choices, modeling decisions, evaluation approaches, and failure modes. This phase targets the gap between LLM-generated written work and actual understanding: Students cannot improvise consistent answers about decisions in work they did not personally complete.

  3. Case discussion agent: Discusses one case study from a library of real-world AI/ML product cases covered in the semester, asking questions that span course topics. In Fall 2025, the agent itself selected the case from a prompt-supplied library; in Spring 2026, the case is drawn in code from a per-session random seed and passed to the agent as a dynamic variable. The agent generates its questions dynamically during the examination.

Only per-session dynamic variables flow across hand-offs, not prior-phase transcript text; the downstream grading council still sees the full concatenated transcript. The failure modes originate in the underlying LLM, not the voice platform, so the patterns that address them surface on any stack that delegates conversation management to a language model (voice selection travels less easily; Appendix K).

Grading: A council of LLMs.  We implemented a “council of LLMs”: three models from different families independently score the same transcript, then revise after seeing each other’s reasoning. We used Claude, Gemini, and GPT-5, one from each of the three major frontier-model families available at deployment rather than a tuned panel size.c This “LLM-as-judge” approach extends a long history of automated scoring19 to oral examination transcripts: Language models evaluate open-ended work in place of human raters21,22 and can debate their judgments in multi-agent exchanges.2 The process has three steps:

  1. Round 1 (Independent): Each model receives the full examination transcript and the grading rubric, then independently scores it on the rubric’s dimensions (in our case, five dimensions, each scored 0–4), with verbatim transcript evidence for each score: Problem Framing (business problem → ML spec), Metrics & Economics (evaluation metrics, trade-offs, counter-metrics), Risk & Ethics (failure modes; fairness, accountability, transparency, privacy, security), Experimentation (A/B design, hypotheses, controls), and Communication (structured answers under follow-up pushback). The three models run in parallel with no shared context.

  2. Round 2 (Deliberation): Each model receives the other two models’ complete Round 1 output (their per-dimension scores, written justifications, and the verbatim transcript excerpts each one cited) rather than a paraphrased digest, and is asked to revise its own evaluation in light of that reasoning. We label peers neutrally (“Peer 1,” “Peer 2”) and withhold model identities, so a model cannot defer to a brand rather than an argument.d Models may change scores or reaffirm them, but must justify either decision with transcript evidence. On one Spring 2026 exam (a DocuSign “Contract Risk Analyzer” project), a grader who had scored Problem Framing higher revised it down to 3 once a peer noted the student had never worked through the project’s second-order effects, arguing the change from what the transcript showed rather than from the peer’s number.

  3. Chair Synthesis: A designated chair model (Claude) receives all Round 1 and Round 2 outputs and produces the final grade: one score per dimension, a total score (0–20), and a structured feedback report with strengths, weaknesses, and verbatim evidence.

Why not use a single model? Because initial independent assessments showed poor agreement; the deliberation phase was necessary. A known risk is anchoring bias: When models see each other’s Round 1 scores, they may converge toward a shared (possibly wrong) answer rather than genuinely revising. We cannot rule this out, but the deliberation transcripts show substantive engagement: Models cite specific transcript evidence to argue for score changes rather than splitting differences. The convergence reads as reasoning, not anchoring. The full grading prompt and a worked deliberation example are in Appendix B.

Deployment and Results

We deployed the system as the final examination for an undergraduate AI/ML Product Management course at NYU Stern across two consecutive cohorts, Fall 2025 (36 students) and Spring 2026 (37 students), with fixes shipped between them. We use the semester labels throughout to line up with the dated tables and figures.

The system eliminated scheduling as a constraint; students chose any time during a nine-day window in each cohort (Table 1 lists the opening dates). Students recorded themselves (webcam and audio) during the examination as a course requirement, both to deter outsourcing or real-time assistance and as a backup if the conversational pipeline failed mid-exam. This exam-integrity obligation is separate from research consent: Under IRB protocol NYU IRB-FY2023-7595, de-identified transcripts and survey responses enter the analysis only for consenting students; a student who declined would still have taken the exam for course assessment, with their data excluded from the study. No student in either cohort declined.

Cost.  Two regimes matter. Within our $99/month ElevenLabs subscription, which covered all voice minutes in both cohorts, the per-exam marginal cost reduces to grading-LLM API calls alone: ∼$0.29 per Fall 2025 exam (billed) and ∼$0.96 per Spring 2026 exam (estimated; Appendix E), or $0.01–$0.03 per student-minute. The Spring jump is a configuration choice, not a scaling signal: a Claude Opus 4.6 chair accounted for roughly two-thirds of grading spend; reverting to a cheaper chair tier would halve the total. Above an equivalent subscription credit pool, voice bills at the ElevenLabs additional-call overage rate of $0.08 per agent-minute, so the planning figure is roughly $0.11 per student-minute, or about $3.40 for a 30-minute graded exam (before retry/setup overhead).

These per-exam figures are the marginal cost. The larger cost is a one-time adaptation: writing the rubric, curating the case library, and authoring the per-phase questions. The orchestration and grading platform already exists (we now run it as a hosted service), so this is exam-authoring effort rather than a systems-engineering burden, the same rubric-and-question work a written or in-person exam requires. In our deployments, authoring a new exam and rubric took roughly four to eight hours, and we would not expect more than a day or two even for a wholly new discipline. Much of that authoring is itself AI-assistable, shared across a course’s other assessments, and amortized over every exam that reuses it (Appendix E).

Grading reliability.  Initial independent grading in Fall 2025 revealed an inconsistency: Gemini averaged 16.3/20 while Claude averaged 13.0/20, a 3.3-point gap (GPT-5 fell between at 13.7/20, within one point of Claude on 64% of students). Without deliberation, the council was useless. After deliberation, convergence was asymmetric: Gemini dropped its mean by 1.3 points after seeing stricter peer assessments, Claude rose by 0.9, GPT-5 by 0.3, all three converging toward the 14–15 range. That the largest shift came from the most lenient model suggests substantive revision rather than score-splitting.

Deliberation improves agreement, with the largest relative gain in the noisier Fall 2025 cohort (Figure 2; per-dimension breakdown in Appendix L, Figure 6). Perfect three-way agreement rose from 29% to 74% in Fall 2025 and from 49% to 86% in Spring 2026 (pooled across the five rubric dimensions); 2+ point spreads fell from 11% to 1% (Fall 2025) and from 1% to 0% (Spring 2026). We summarize agreement with Krippendorff’s α, a chance-corrected agreement score on a 0–1 scale: It discounts the agreement three raters would reach just by guessing, so it is a stricter bar than the raw percentages above. On that scale, α≥0.80 is the conventional threshold for good agreement;13 we compute α following.14 Pooled the same way, α rose from 0.52→0.86 in Fall 2025 and 0.65→0.90 in Spring 2026. On the 0–20 overall score, it reached 0.83 and 0.95 after deliberation.

Pooled α above threshold does not say where the residual disagreement lives. Decomposing the council shows that a single rater accounts for nearly all of it, as a directional offset: In both cohorts, Gemini is more lenient on the 0–20 total (Gemini – Claude signed mean: +1.08 Fall 2025, +0.38 Spring 2026), while Claude and GPT-5 agree almost perfectly (pairwise α=0.97 and 0.99). Dropping Gemini would lift overall-score α to 0.97 and 0.99, yet we retain Gemini deliberately: A persistently lenient voice forces the stricter raters to cite specific transcript evidence rather than reaffirm low scores by default (Appendix I). We added human audit as a core step: Flag an exam when Claude and GPT-5 diverge by more than one point on the 0–20 scale, or when Gemini sits more than two points from the midpoint of Claude and GPT-5. In Spring 2026, this rule fires on roughly 3% of exams (Appendix J). The practical lesson: Expect per-model biases to survive deliberation as stable offsets and choose raters for argumentative asymmetry rather than interchangeability.

Diagnostic power for teaching quality.  Reliability (“Do raters agree?”) is necessary but not sufficient; validity (“Do grades reflect actual student competence?”) requires expert human judgment. As a partial validity check, the instructor and TA graded all 36 Fall 2025 exams independently; the instructor’s initial grades sat close to Gemini’s, but on review the instructor conceded most of the stricter council scores once cited transcript evidence was visible. The same evidence trail benefits students directly: Every exam yields a structured, evidence-linked feedback report as a byproduct of grading, something human graders rarely produce for every student (Appendix M). External grading has a second side benefit over instructor self-grading: It surfaces teaching deficiencies that would otherwise remain hidden.

Scores by topic varied (Figure 3): Fall 2025 Experimentation (A/B testing) averaged 1.94/4 with a left tail (8% scored 0, 19% scored 1, zero demonstrated mastery), against Problem Framing at 3.39/4. This was a mirror held up to the instructors, not just the students: A/B testing had received insufficient class time, easy to overlook when instructors grade their own students leniently on topics they know were covered superficially. The gap closed in Spring 2026 after we rebalanced the syllabus: Experimentation rose to 2.70, with no student scoring below 2.

Duration was a poor proxy for score in both cohorts (Figure 4): The shortest Fall 2025 exam (9 minutes) earned the highest score (19/20), while the longest (41 minutes) earned one of the lowest (12/20). In Spring 2026, the trend was moderately negative.

What Broke: What We Wish We Knew Before Deploying

Fall 2025 surfaced five failure modes: The agent stacked several questions into a single turn; it paraphrased questions when asked to repeat them; it treated a student’s thinking pause as a dropped call; it selected case studies far from randomly; and, in a cloned professor’s voice, it came across as harsh. Some we fixed in code for Spring 2026, some we could only mitigate at the prompt level, and one (silence as thinking) survived its fix. Each part below gives the problem, then what we changed, and for the surviving one, why it resisted.

Question stacking.  The most damaging issue. The agent regularly fired off compound questions. From an actual transcript: “Tighten it up for me: who is the user, and what decision do they make differently because of your product? And what is your North Star metric, plus one counter metric that might get worse if you over-optimize?” A Fall 2025 student summed it up: “It kept asking 3 to 4 questions at the same time, despite me asking it to slow down multiple times.” More than half of the student improvement suggestions on the exit survey mentioned this problem. Prompt-level instructions helped but did not eliminate the behavior: For constraining LLM behavior in extended conversations, they are necessary but insufficient. The failure is not unique to our stack: Socratic Mind’s authors observed the same multi-question drift and planned a prompt-level fix.9 We also built an “interference protocol” into the grading rubric, instructing graders to assess only the answered parts when the agent stacked questions and the student answered only some.

The lesson: Enforce behavioral constraints through system architecture, not just prompting. Spring 2026 added a programmatic turn validator that detects a multi-question turn and asks the model to re-emit a single-question version. The rate of stacked turns (a single agent turn packing in two or more separate questions) fell from 31% in Fall 2025 to 11% in Spring 2026.e The turns that remained also got simpler: Three-or-more-question turns nearly vanished, falling from 2.9% to 0.3%; questions spanning two rubric dimensions roughly halved, from 10.6% to 4.6%; and the median stacked turn shrank from 52 to 38 words. A few three- and four-question turns still surface, so this is a large reduction, not an elimination.

Paraphrasing during clarification.  When students asked the agent to repeat a question, it would paraphrase rather than repeat verbatim, inadvertently changing the question. The LLM was doing what it was trained to do (being helpful by rephrasing) but exactly the wrong reflex in an examination. Explicit prompt instructions (“repeat the exact previous question”) reduced but did not eliminate the behavior; this remains a prompt-level mitigation, not a code-enforced one.

Silence handling.  By default, the platform treated a silence as a sign that something had gone wrong (a dropped call) rather than as a student thinking. Fall 2025 ran on the 5 seconds default, so the agent would cut in with “Are you there?” exactly when a student was formulating an answer. Spring 2026 raised the threshold to 15 seconds, but the interruptions persisted, and students reported that the check-ins spiked their stress precisely when they were trying to think. The lesson: silence is thinking time. Our default for future semesters is 30 seconds.

Non-random case selection.  This was the most instructive failure (Figure 5). The examination prompt listed eight case studies and instructed the agent to “randomly select ONE case.” From Dec. 12–17, when the Zillow case study (Zillow’s iBuyer home-buying program, used to discuss concept drift and adverse selection) was on the list, the agent selected it in 6 of 7 examinations (86%). At the end of Dec. 18, we removed this case study from the prompt. The agent immediately shifted to the Predictive Policing case study, selecting it for 14 of 22 examinations on Dec. 19–20 (64%), better than the level of fixation on the Zillow case study but still far from the ∼14% expected under uniform selection over the remaining seven cases. A predictable case is also a leakable one: A student who can anticipate which case they will receive can prepare that scenario in advance or tip off the next student, undercutting the leak-resistance that the dynamically generated questions otherwise give the format.

The fundamental issue: LLMs should not be trusted to implement uniform randomization by instruction. The same deterministic bias appears when models are asked simply to generate random numbers.4 They carry ordering biases that survive every prompt-level mitigation we tried, and the bias is invisible until you examine the output distribution. Kelly12 makes the broader case that randomization is routinely botched even when practitioners are explicitly trying to implement it; asking an LLM to randomize by instruction is a textbook instance. The fix is to draw a random number in code and map it to a case deterministically, which is what Spring 2026 shipped. Across the 37 Spring 2026 examinations, all eight cases were used and the maximum single-case share was 22% (8/37), in contrast to the Fall 2025 single-week 86% peak.f The principle generalizes: Any behavior requiring uniformity or randomness belongs in code, not in the LLM.

Voice characteristics.  We cloned the voice of a course professor from a conference keynote, reasoning that a familiar voice would feel more natural than the defaults. The opposite happened: Students described the agent as “aggressive,” “condescending,” “shouting,” a “sports coach” style “absolutely not appropriate for classroom use.” One free-response answer reduced it to four words: “Make it less mean.” Keynote delivery (fast-paced, projected, designed to talk at a large audience) is the wrong register for a one-on-one exam; without the softening cues of face-to-face interaction, a high-fidelity clone of an authority figure read as intimidating rather than familiar. Spring 2026 switched to “Alice,” an ElevenLabs preset with a calm, education-oriented register; the change removed the complaints. Voice characteristics warrant the same attention as question design.

Table 2 collects the five patterns, pairing each with the failure it addresses and the implementation that enforced the fix; paraphrasing remains the one failure without an architectural pattern, mitigated only at the prompt level.

Student Experience

The central tension held in both cohorts: what the exam measured well versus how it felt to take. Fall 2025 students rated “tested my actual understanding” highest (70% agreement), but only 33% found questions clear and 83% found the exam more stressful than written exams. Spring 2026 replicated the student-perceived-understanding finding (66%) while clarity rose to 78% and “more stressful” fell to 63%; the timing coincides with the between-cohort engineering fixes, though with several changes at once we cannot say which fix moved which response. “Tested my actual understanding” is a student-perceived measure, not a psychometric validity claim.

These rates come from voluntary surveys run after the exam but before grade release (30 of 36 responding in Fall 2025, 32 of 37 in Spring 2026; the instrument and full response distributions are in Appendices C and D). Such surveys can over-represent polarized reactions, so we checked the one thing we observe for non-respondents, their final grades: In both cohorts, they were statistically indistinguishable from respondents’ (Appendix D.4). Prior oral-exam experience does not appear to explain the stress response: The share who had never taken an oral exam held flat across cohorts while the stress rate fell (cross-tabulations in Appendix D.2). Format preference was more consistent with perceived stress than with prior oral-exam experience: The share preferring an AI oral exam rose from 13% to 25%. Comfort and fairness ratings rose, too, so rising trust in AI may also be at work.

The most praised feature in both cohorts was scheduling flexibility. The most common Fall 2025 complaint was question stacking, matching the 31% stacked-turn rate; the complaint receded in Spring 2026 free responses as the rate dropped to roughly 11%.

Accessibility cut both ways. Some Fall 2025 students with anxiety-related accommodations volunteered that they found the AI examiner less stressful than typical exams, suggesting the format could serve as a test-anxiety accommodation in some populations. For international students, the format cut the other way: “At times, the difficulty wasn’t in knowing the material but in articulating my thoughts under pressure in English.” We added a live transcript display for Spring 2026 in response to Fall 2025 requests; it lets students catch mistranscriptions in real time, but cognitive load under pressure remains (caveats and a fuller accessibility discussion in Appendix M).

One complaint increased in Spring 2026: The adaptive nature of questioning was perceived as “unfair;” students want exam difficulty to be the same for everyone. Asked to agree or disagree that the examiner “felt like a fair evaluator,” 33% agreed in Fall 2025 and 56% in Spring 2026. Yet, after grades were released, only two regrading requests came in, both Fall 2025, and no points were conceded in either case. The complaint was about process, not outcome.

Discussion

For anyone considering adoption, three gains hold even with audit overhead: The system automates the time-dominant interview phase, concentrates human review on high-disagreement cases, and makes oral assessment operationally feasible at cohort sizes where a faculty-administered oral is not. At those sizes, the realistic counterfactual is not AI-vs-human but AI-vs-written-only; the fuller argument is in Appendix G. The caveats start with what the grades mean. The grading council’s high agreement establishes reliability (consistency among AI raters), not validity (correctness against expert judgment); the human auditor on roughly 3% of Spring 2026 exams is a guardrail, not a full fix. What we can claim is operational feasibility and promising reliability. What we cannot claim is that these grades carry the validity of a well-run faculty oral, or that the format is demonstrably fair to every student: The first would take blinded expert re-grading, the second a subgroup fairness analysis, and we have performed neither.

The format inverts the traditional cheating incentive. The LLM generates questions dynamically against published guidelines rather than from a fixed question bank, so there is no exam to leak. Practicing against the published structure is itself the learning behavior the format rewards. Two academic-dishonesty vectors still deserve treatment in the unsupervised home environment: live AI coaching via a headset or phone (not fully preventable; a broader societal concern), and a confederate in the room (deterred by the self-recorded video requirement). The vector-by-vector detail is in Appendix H.

Voice-based assessment introduces accessibility trade-offs that a written format avoids. Speaking under time pressure adds cognitive load and can disadvantage students who articulate or process more slowly, or whose accented speech is transcribed less accurately; students with speech-related disabilities face barriers a keyboard would not impose. In practice, speech recognition handled the technical course vocabulary well, and because the speech-to-text output feeds an LLM that already has the course context, the system can in principle repair some accented-speech errors. But we did not measure word error rate against gold references and cannot quantify the residual. These trade-offs call for explicit accommodations: extended or configurable time limits, a choice of voice and speaking pace, an ungraded practice run to defuse unfamiliarity, and a text-based alternative for students who cannot use voice. We detail these, alongside Spring 2026’s live-transcript mitigation, in Appendix M.

Finally, data governance. The system transmits voice audio and transcripts to ElevenLabs and graded-transcript text to Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI for council grading, governed by each provider’s API privacy policy and (where available) by enterprise/zero-retention agreements; we did not run an independent audit. Locally recorded webcam and audio (a course-integrity requirement) are not transmitted to any vendor. Appendix M covers feedback quality and what a human examination provides that this system loses.

Conclusion

The spread of LLMs has disrupted traditional assessment. Rather than pursuing a detection arms race, we can adopt formats that inherently reward actual understanding. Oral examinations have always had this property but never scaled; voice AI restores scalability. Our deployment demonstrates operational feasibility across two cohorts (73 students). Agreement within the grading council is high. That is encouraging, but it does not by itself settle validity against double-blind expert human graders. Student experience was mixed. Students felt the exams tested their understanding but found them more stressful than written exams; the “more stressful” rate fell from the first cohort to the second as engineering fixes shipped, and question stacking, the most-cited culprit, fell with it. They dislike the adaptive nature of questioning as procedurally unfair; yet, once grades were released, almost no one disputed them.

The practical contribution is the five patterns collected in Table 2. Two iterations were enough to surface them; how far they carry is what we hope future deployments will show. The same infrastructure has an application beyond the final exam: Attaching a short oral comprehension check to every written assignment would convert the system from a semester-end assessment tool into a continuous authenticity layer (Appendix N).

The online supplement includes the voice-agent and grading-council prompts and a sanitized snapshot of the code; the anonymized data and analysis scripts are archived at Zenodo.g Deploy it, use it, and report back what works and what breaks.

More Online

Appendices are available in the online supplemental material: https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3831714.

Acknowledgments

We thank Brian Jabarian for discussions on AI-administered interviews, Foster Provost for voice contribution, and Andrej Karpathy for the council-of-LLMs concept. Approved under NYU IRB-FY2023-7595.
